content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) initiated abortion surveillance in 1969 to systematically document the number and characteristics of women undergoing legal induced abortions. This surveillance relies on data voluntarily reported by states and jurisdictions, which conduct their own abortion data collection efforts. The CDC compiles this information to create a comprehensive dataset on legal induced abortions. For surveillance purposes, the CDC defines a legal induced abortion as an intervention performed by a licensed clinician—such as a physician, nurse-midwife, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant—within the boundaries of state regulations. The procedure is intended to terminate a suspected or confirmed ongoing intrauterine pregnancy and does not result in a live birth. This definition specifically excludes procedures related to the management of intrauterine fetal death, early pregnancy failure or loss, ectopic pregnancy, or retained products of conception. Most states and jurisdictions that collect abortion data also report whether the procedure was performed using medication or surgery. It is important to note that states and jurisdictions are not mandated to report abortion data to the CDC. Participation in the CDC’s abortion surveillance system is entirely voluntary. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health compiles and analyzes the data provided to produce the annual Abortion Surveillance report. States and jurisdictions seeking guidance on abortion surveillance can contact the CDC for assistance. The preparation of the Abortion Surveillance report involves analyzing data submitted by states and jurisdictions for a specific calendar year. Once the data is received, CDC staff conduct analyses to generate tables, figures, and narratives that describe the methods and trends observed. Detailed information on the compilation process can be found in the abstract and methods section of the most recent Abortion Surveillance report. The Abortion Surveillance report serves several critical public health purposes. It is used to evaluate the effectiveness of programs designed to promote equitable access to high-quality, patient-centered contraceptive services in the United States, with the goal of reducing unintended pregnancies. Additionally, the report helps calculate pregnancy rates by combining abortion data with birth data and estimates of pregnancy loss. It also monitors changes in clinical practices related to abortion, such as shifts in the types of procedures performed and the gestational age at which abortions occur. Furthermore, the report is used to calculate the national case-fatality rate for legal induced abortions. For those interested in conducting their own analyses, data from the annual Abortion Surveillance report is available, including datasets spanning from 2012 to 2021.
